Issued at 338 AM CDT Fri Oct 23 2026

Wind and fire weather concerns are the main highlights today.

Currently, surface low pressure was situated over western
Montana with a moderate southerly surface flow over western and
central ND. Skies ranged from clear to partly cloudy over the
area, with mild temperatures in the mid 40s to mid 50s.

For today, the northern portion of a splitting upper level 
trough to our west will lift into central Montana, with a 
surface low situated over the ND/MT border near Sidney Montana
by 00 UTC Saturday. A warm front will extend southeast from the
low through south central ND, allowing for very warm
temperatures in southwest and south central ND. Record highs 
will be possible at Dickinson and Bismarck this afternoon. A 
passing shower is possible today as strong warm advection lifts 
through the state, but qpf amounts would be insignificant (a 
trace to a hundredth or two). Better chances for precip will be 
limited to the northwest tonight where some light post-frontal 
rain could occur. 

Fire weather concerns increase in the southwest this afternoon.
Will cover this in the Fire Weather section below.

As the upper level trough and associated surface low lifts
northward into Canada, a strong cold front will move quickly 
east through western and central ND. This will bring a period of
strong west to northwest winds to the forecast area tonight 
into Saturday morning, and possibly lingering into the afternoon
over the north central. Overall, there was little change in the
specifics with this system, when compared to 24 hours ago. The 
max winds at the top of the boundary layer are perhaps a little 
lower, but the strength of the cold advection and the strength 
and placement of the fall-rise couplet are very similar. Bufkit 
soundings indicate 45-50 knots of wind atop a well mixed 
boundary layer that could potentially work down to the surface. 
The timing of the cold front passage is not ideal. The depth of
the unidirectional flow and the steep lapse rates is right 
around 850 mb, so this could be better too. The strength and 
track of the initial shortwave is not ideal either. On the other
hand, the amount of cold advection and the magnitude of the 
isallobaric change is short lived, but impressive. Initial 
thoughts are that we may need a wind advisory tonight over a 
portion of the forecast area. Given that the initial push of 
strong winds will not be until tonight in the west, we will hold
off on issuing any headlines at this time. The orientation of 
the 850 jet as well as the upper level jet tonight would suggest
that western and north central ND would be the areas most 
likely to see sustained advisory criteria winds. As you get into
south central ND you get farther away from the strongest winds 
and the greatest isallobaric component. Cold advection also 
drops off a bit. With the late timing and uncertainties 
remaining, will let the day shift take another look.

Winds drop off quickly from west to east Saturday. Advisory
criteria winds could be done before midday for most areas. The
far northern tier counties, and especially around the Turtle
Mountains, could see stronger winds linger into the afternoon.

Much cooler on Saturday with highs in the mid 40s to mid 50s. 
Temperatures then remain nearly steady, near to a little below 
normal Sunday and into next week.

The southern portion aforementioned splitting upper level
trough, lingers over the southwest U.S. a bit then lifts into
the Central/Northern Plains early in the work week. There is
some uncertainty as to how far north this system makes it, but
at least southern portions of the forecast area could see some
low to medium chances for light precipitation. With our cooler 
temperatures in place, there will be a chance of a mix of rain 
and snow late Sunday night into Monday morning, and again late 
Monday night into Tuesday morning. Another upper level system 
may bring additional precipitation chances into the area by mid
to late in the workweek.
